value: consistently swim away from static magnetic fields over 20 µT (radial arm maze, constant magnet position and changing magnet position)
method: behavioural: glass catfish in a three-arm radial (Y-type) maze with a neodymium magnet placed 10 cm from the end of one arm; the number of fish in each arm was counted once per second from overhead video; the field at the arm was modelled (COMSOL), not measured, and the 20 µT figure is read from that model
conditions: 13 glass catfish of undetermined sex and age tested as a group (a school), the same fish across the constant-location and changing-location experiments (12 in the latter); magnet surface flux 577 mT; 30-minute trials, each condition repeated four times, 24 trials in all; constant-location design: fish started in a randomly assigned arm and the magnet was always in Arm 1; changing-location design: fish held in the centre and the stimulus placed in a random arm; a sham of plastic and aluminum foil matching the magnet's dimensions was run, and as read through a page-summary tool the Results report fewer fish in the sham arm than in the arms without a stimulus in the constant-location design, while the Discussion reports no avoidance of the sham in the single-fish and alternating-location trials, so avoidance of the magnet arm is not fully separated from avoidance of an object placed at that arm; no baseline count in Arm 1 before the magnet was added is reported; Mann-Whitney U tests on arm occupancy; fish acclimatized 6 weeks after arrival from Thailand, kept in a 30-gallon tank on a 12 h day/night cycle at 27 C, fed brine shrimp twice daily, tested 11 am to 4 pm; anaesthesia not mentioned; arms oriented to offset Earth's field; no tested field range below 20 µT is claimed as a limit

source.authors: Hunt RD, Ashbaugh RC, Reimers M, Udpa L, Saldana De Jimenez G, Moore M, Gilad AA, Pelled G
source.title: Swimming direction of the glass catfish is responsive to magnetic stimulation

quote: The results demonstrate that glass catfish placed in a radial arm maze, consistently swim away from magnetic fields over 20 μT and show adaptability to changing magnetic field direction and location.
note: Abstract and Results read on the PLOS ONE article page through WebFetch (CC BY printed: 'distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License'; Crossref gives CC BY 4.0); the page summariser caps quotes near 125 characters, so the abstract sentence was assembled from two consecutive pieces and was not machine-checked. The Results state the 20 µT figure as 'glass catfish prefer to avoid swimming in water with a magnetic strength over 20 μT (Figs 1c and 2)'. Crossref: no correction, preprint 10.1101/2020.08.13.250035 exists. Kryptopterus vitreolus is absent from docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv; family Siluridae is given from memory of Eschmeyer's Catalog and needs the owner check (see owner questions). The paper notes the species was previously called K. bicirrhis.

method: anatomical: interommatidial angle calculated as facet diameter divided by the local radius of curvature of the eye, with the radius computed from eye-segment baseline length and height; facet diameter from scanning electron microscopy
conditions: Adults collected from the campus of Henan University of Science and Technology, Henan Province, China, in May 2023; 40 adults (20 females, 20 males) used for the morphological work, sexes pooled for the optical analyses because no significant dimorphism was found; heads taken from live adults after diethyl ether anaesthesia and fixed in 2% paraformaldehyde and 2.5% glutaraldehyde (fixation shrinkage not assessed); facet diameter 24.45 ± 0.30 µm (females, n = 8) and 24.43 ± 0.35 µm (males, n = 8), eye diameter n = 3 per sex, other measurements n = 6 per sex; the number of eyes behind the 4.08 degree value is not stated in the text read; no optical, ophthalmoscopic or behavioural measurement of resolution; the Results section points to Table 1 and the value is quoted here from the Abstract (the Discussion repeats it as larger than the 1 to 3 degrees of most flying insects)

source.authors: Chen Q-X, Li Y-F, Huo Y-Z
source.title: Unraveling the Compound Eye Design of the Diurnal Moth Histia flabellicornis (Lepidoptera: Zygaenidae)

quote: The calculated interommatidial angles (Δϕ = 4.08°) and the eye parameter P (P = 1.74) suggest a visual system adapted to moderate light conditions, balancing spatial resolution with photon capture.
note: Calculated from anatomy by the authors, not a measured behavioural or optical angle; the quote names no species, tied to Histia flabellicornis by the paper's title. Read on the MDPI article page through WebFetch (rights field CC BY 3.0 on the page, Crossref gives CC BY 4.0, version of record); Crossref: no correction. The abstract sentence was assembled from two consecutive pieces returned by the page summariser and was not machine-checked. Histia flabellicornis is absent from docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (see owner questions).

method: behavioural: two-alternative forced choice between an LCD field showing a single dot and a blank field, food-rewarded; single target acuity (smallest dot angle) by the method of constant stimuli, six dot sizes, 30 presentations per size, 75% correct threshold interpolated; the paper converts the minimum visual angle to a grating resolution in cycles per degree
conditions: Full-contrast condition (C1); six common sunfish (two males, four females, aged 11 to 12 years, 8 to 11 cm long) that had taken part in earlier visual experiments, each housed alone and tested in its own 240-litre aquarium (120 x 40 x 55 cm) facing an LCD monitor, background 131.83 cd m-2, dot sizes measured in underwater photographs as full width at half amplitude; reward two to three red mosquito larvae per correct choice; each threshold used five 36-trial sessions (180 trials); pretraining at Weber contrast 0.97; the quoted value is the mean of five fish (0.13 to 0.18 degrees, mean ± s.d. 0.14 ± 0.02 degrees); the sixth fish (named Anna) had a significantly higher threshold of 0.32 degrees and is excluded from this mean, so the abstract's all-six value is 0.17 degrees (0.13 to 0.32 degrees); the paper reports no all-six mean; whether the ± on 3.6 ± 0.5 is s.d. is not labelled in the text read; the viewing distance used for the angle is not stated in the text read; reduced-contrast thresholds (C2 0.34 ± 0.02 degrees, C3 0.42 ± 0.08 degrees) are separate findings and not claimed here; a single dot is not a grating, so the cycles per degree figure is the authors' conversion

source.authors: Spratte C, Sandow L-M, Schnermann JS, Hanke FD
source.title: Single target acuity in the common sunfish (Lepomis gibbosus)

quote: STA for the five other fish ranged between 0.13 and 0.18 deg with a mean±s.d. value of 0.14±0.02 deg corresponding to a grating resolution of 3.6±0.5 cycles deg−1 with no significant difference among individuals (Kruskal–Wallis test, P>0.05).
note: Read on the publisher's own free full-text page (cob.silverchair.com, Company of Biologists) through WebFetch without a login; the page prints only the publisher copyright, no licence line; Crossref lists the biologists.com user licence (vor), no correction. 'STA' is the paper's abbreviation for single target acuity. Quote assembled from three consecutive pieces and the sentence end confirmed by a second read of the page, not machine-checked. A separate paper by Hoppe et al. 2024 (Biology Open) on moving targets in the same species was not opened. Lepomis gibbosus is absent from docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (see owner questions).

value: median best-response electric field at which rays oriented to a prey-simulating dipole: 0.006 µV/cm in the brackish-saltwater (BSW) group and 1.4 µV/cm in the freshwater (FW) group
method: behavioural: a ray's response was scored from video when it oriented to an active dipole (4 dipoles, one energised at random, current 6.9 to 8.3 µA); the field at the orientation point was calculated with the ideal dipole equation from the orientation distance and angle, not measured; each ray's best (weakest-field) response was used
conditions: Atlantic stingray (published as Dasyatis sabina) from two populations, Indian River Lagoon (estuarine) and St Johns River (Lake Harney, freshwater); 51 rays collected, 7 excluded for lack of feeding motivation, 44 analysed (the collection counts in the text do not reconcile to 51; per-treatment n not read); unrestrained, no anaesthesia, in a 122 x 244 x 50 cm fibreglass tank, acclimated at least 10 min to the tank and fed at least 7 days at each test salinity (salinity changed 2 ppt per 24 h); St Johns River rays were tested in a fixed order (0, then 15, then 35 ppt) and the 35 ppt group was dropped after 60% mortality, Indian River Lagoon rays were tested at capture salinity (7 brackish rays acclimated to freshwater); randomisation applied only to which dipole was energised; thawed shrimp used to arouse feeding; no sham or no-stimulus control described; stimulus frequency not stated; the abstract states the freshwater rays needed a field 200 to 300 times larger (median FW 1.4 µV/cm, median brackish-saltwater 6 nV/cm) and a maximum orientation distance 35.2% shorter (44.0 cm to 28.5 cm); weakest fields detected 0.0006 µV/cm (Indian River Lagoon, 35 ppt) and 0.2 µV/cm (Indian River Lagoon, 0 ppt) as read through a page summary

source.title: Electroreception in the euryhaline stingray, Dasyatis sabina

quote: The median electric fields for the BSW (0.006 μVcm–1) and FW (1.4 μVcm–1) groups were derived from the best responses for each stingray in their respective treatment.
note: Read on the publisher's own free full-text page (cob.silverchair.com, Company of Biologists) through WebFetch, no login; the page prints no licence line and Crossref lists none for this DOI (no correction either). The sentence reports medians of best responses, not a statistical threshold. Quote assembled from two consecutive pieces and not machine-checked. Taxon given as the accepted Hypanus sabinus (docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv lists Dasyatis sabina as a synonym); the paper uses Dasyatis sabina; family Dasyatidae from memory of Eschmeyer, to be confirmed.

value: evidence of four sensitivity peaks, in the ranges 380-420 nm (violet), 440-480 nm, 500-600 nm and 600-680 nm, with maximal sensitivity at longer wavelengths
method: electrophysiological: ERG b-wave and optic nerve compound action potentials recorded from isolated eyecups superfused with Ringer's solution at 20 ± 1 C; sensitivity taken as the -log10 photon irradiance giving a half-maximal response (Hill fit to response-intensity curves)
conditions: Adult Nile tilapia (150 days post-fertilisation or older, 19.5 to 26.4 cm total length, 140 to 333.5 g) from a commercial fish farm in Ontario, strain not stated; total number of fish not stated, figure legends give N = 3 to 7 per data point and N = 4 for most points under the long-wavelength adapting backgrounds; each eyecup adapted for 25 to 30 min to a white background or to long-wavelength adapting backgrounds (600LP or 650LP) before recording; the 380-420 nm peak persisted under the long-wavelength backgrounds, which the authors attribute to a violet-sensitive cone mechanism and not to the b-band of the long-wavelength cone; lens transmittance falls steeply between 410 and 380 nm; spectral sensitivity curves recorded at different times of year indicated A1/A2 chromophore shifts; fish killed by clove oil immersion, no anaesthesia during recording; these are ranges of peaks from in-vitro eyecups, not microspectrophotometric lambda max values of single cone classes

source.authors: Lisney TJ, Studd E, Hawryshyn CW
source.title: Electrophysiological assessment of spectral sensitivity in adult Nile tilapia Oreochromis niloticus: evidence for violet sensitivity

quote: We used electrophysiology to assess spectral sensitivity in this species and found evidence of four sensitivity peaks in the ranges 380–420, 440–480, 500–600 and 600–680 nm, with maximal sensitivity at longer wavelengths.
note: Read on the publisher's own free PDF (cob.silverchair.com, Company of Biologists) through WebFetch, no login; the copy prints only the publisher copyright and Crossref lists no licence for this DOI (no correction). Quote assembled from two consecutive pieces and not machine-checked. The value is a set of ranges that the source gives; no single lambda max is claimed. Oreochromis niloticus is absent from docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (see owner questions); main holds only a near-infrared spectral_range row for this species (10.1371/journal.pone.0064429), a different finding.

value: intensity threshold of colour vision (mean) 0.4 cd/m2
method: behavioural: green versus blue colour discrimination at falling luminance, 65% correct criterion
conditions: Behavioural choice test: birds trained to take a positive green stimulus over a negative blue one at 252 cd m-2 (criterion at least 75% correct in two consecutive 20-trial sets, wrong choices not punished); each bird then made 60 choices at each of 6 to 9 luminance levels (252 down to 0.0156 cd m-2), adapted 10 to 15 min before each session; threshold = the luminance giving 65% correct, interpolated from the choice curves (binomial, N = 60, P < 0.05); ten stimulus pairs, five with green brighter than blue, built from quantum catch so that a brightness-only choice gives 50% correct, each pair used twice in random order and side; cage in a completely dark room lit by fluorescent tubes and LEDs; wild-type coloured birds from local breeders, ages not stated; the number of birds in the behavioural test is not given in the text read (at least two Bourke's parrots, since one performed much worse than another); no ± given for the means; the comparison value for people is cited from the literature (0.02 cd m-2); if the worst performing Bourke's parrot is excluded the mean falls to 0.2 cd m-2, still above the budgerigar value (Results); the quoted sentence gives both species, and this record takes the Bourke's parrot half

source.title: The intensity threshold of colour vision in two species of parrot

quote: Mean intensity threshold of colour vision was higher in Bourke's parrots (0.4 cd m–2) than in budgerigars (0.1 cd m–2; Fig. 2).
note: Read on the publisher's own free full-text page (cob.silverchair.com, Company of Biologists) through WebFetch, no login; the page text read prints no licence line and Crossref lists none (no correction). Quote assembled from two consecutive pieces and not machine-checked. Family Psittaculidae follows the family main uses for Melopsittacus; the species is in gbif-names.tsv as accepted. The same sentence backs the budgerigar record in this log, as it states a comparison of the two species; no other Bourke's parrot colour-vision threshold is on main.

conditions: Behavioural choice test: birds trained to take a positive green stimulus over a negative blue one at 252 cd m-2 (criterion at least 75% correct in two consecutive 20-trial sets, wrong choices not punished); each bird then made 60 choices at each of 6 to 9 luminance levels (252 down to 0.0156 cd m-2), adapted 10 to 15 min before each session; threshold = the luminance giving 65% correct, interpolated from the choice curves (binomial, N = 60, P < 0.05); ten stimulus pairs, five with green brighter than blue, built from quantum catch so that a brightness-only choice gives 50% correct, each pair used twice in random order and side; cage in a completely dark room lit by fluorescent tubes and LEDs; wild-type coloured birds from local breeders, ages not stated; the number of birds in the behavioural test is not given in the text read (at least two Bourke's parrots, since one performed much worse than another); no ± given for the means; the comparison value for people is cited from the literature (0.02 cd m-2); the budgerigar mean is lower than the Bourke's parrot mean (0.4 cd m-2) and the text read gives no mean excluding an individual for budgerigars; the quoted sentence gives both species, and this record takes the budgerigar half

source.title: The intensity threshold of colour vision in two species of parrot

quote: Mean intensity threshold of colour vision was higher in Bourke's parrots (0.4 cd m–2) than in budgerigars (0.1 cd m–2; Fig. 2).

value: best sensitivity at 1 kHz and 1.4 kHz (33 dB SPL)
method: electrophysiological: auditory brainstem response audiogram; threshold = midpoint between the lowest level with a visible response and the next lower level, scored by three observers blind to frequency (accepted if their spread was under 10 dB)
conditions: Five giant mole-rats (Fukomys mechowii), 1 to 3 years old and born in the colony of the Department of General Zoology, University of Duisburg-Essen, sexes not stated in the text read; anaesthetised with intramuscular ketamine and xylazine (doses in Table S3, not read), body temperature held with a non-electric heating pad; free-field 5 ms pure tones (1 ms rise and fall, 12 per second, averaged over 256 presentations) from a speaker 15 cm from the left pinna, calibrated with a free-field microphone at the ear position and dB SPL; the quoted sentence is a joint sentence for three species (F. anselli 29 dB SPL and F. micklemi 37 dB SPL at 1 kHz); the mean hearing range at 60 dB SPL, 125 Hz to 4 kHz, is a pooled value for the three species and is not claimed here; no brainstem responses to 36 kHz tones in any animal, so 4 kHz is a measured high-frequency cut-off at 60 dB SPL and not a claim about higher untested tones; F. mechowii was predicted to be more sensitive at low frequencies than F. anselli and was not (no significant difference between them); anaesthesia can raise ABR thresholds relative to awake animals

source.authors: Gerhardt P, Henning Y, Begall S, Malkemper EP
source.title: Audiograms of three subterranean rodent species (genus Fukomys) determined by auditory brainstem responses reveal extremely poor high-frequency hearing

quote: Overall sensitivities were low: F. anselli and F. micklemi showed highest sensitivity (F. anselli: 29 dB SPL, F. micklemi: 37 dB SPL) at 1 kHz, and F. mechowii showed highest sensitivity at 1 kHz and 1.4 kHz (33 dB SPL).
note: Read on the publisher's own free PDF (cob.silverchair.com, Company of Biologists) through WebFetch, no login; the copy read printed no licence line; Crossref lists the biologists.com user licence (accepted-manuscript version) for this DOI. Quote assembled from three consecutive pieces and not machine-checked. Fukomys mechowii is accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv.
